At the end of XXXX ( unable to provide exact date, as Navy Federal changed my account numbers as part of the Fraud Alert and Account Recovery process and I can no longer access previous statements ) I received a notification via the Navy Federal Mobile App that money had been taken out of my account. 

When I logged into the app, I saw that {$5000.00} had been withdrawn from my checking account, which came as a surprise as I had never had that much money in my account ever. Shortly after seeing that, I noticed that a new loan had been taken out in my name, and I immediately contacted Navy Federal to begin the Fraud Alert and Account Recovery process. 

I was issued new account numbers for checking and savings account, debit card, credit card, loan numbers. I submitted the first fraud claim that day over the phone with Navy Federal, and the person on the phone said it certainly appeared to be fraudulent activity. 

Fast forward a few weeks, I got a letter in the mail saying that my fraudulent loan claim had been denied as there was " no billing error detected. '' After this, I went to my ( at the time ) local Navy Federal branch in XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX to talk to a representative. 

After reviewing the loan application, the branch representative asked us to step outside for a moment and called into Navy Federal to what I assume was the underwriters to " give them an earful '' for approving what was an obviously fraudulent application. 

The branch representative said that the work place didn't match mine, the application listed assets that were not mine, and told us that the person in XXXX that the loan was " instantly transferred to '' went on a " good little spending spree. '' As a result of this, I filled out and successfully disputed the loan on all three credit bureaus, as well as submitted a report on identitytheft.gov, and put the report numbers on the next appeal, to no avail. 

After this, I went back into the bank to speak to another representative, who told me she " didn't understand why this kept getting denied. '' I went and filled out the paperwork once again with the branch representative and included all the credit bureau information as well as the identitytheft.gov report number, but was denied once more. 

I have also since frozen all my credit on all three bureaus. I am currently stuck in a loop of appealing and getting denied with no information provided as to why, only having what the branch representatives have told me is " clearly fraudulent '' to go off of. 

I am at my wits end, this process has been going on for over three months, and I am not sure what the next steps I need to take are to get this resolved.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am sharing my experience to emphasize the importance of accurate credit reporting and the serious consequences that can occur when errors are not corrected.

I am formally disputing several significant errors on my credit report related to an account with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. These errors include discrepancies in the reported creditors name, missing balance and payment information, inconsistencies in reporting dates, and a lack of transparency regarding account ownership. These inaccuracies have negatively impacted my credit score and overall financial standing. The issues I am raising are of serious concern regarding compliance with the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) and the Fair Credit Billing Act ( FCBA ).

Key Issues : 1. Discrepancy in Creditor Name : The creditors name is inaccurately listed as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, which may not match the correct legal name of the entity. Additionally, the creditor/furnisher consistently identifies itself as " XXXX XXXX XXXX on billing statements, which conflicts with its charter name, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX . This misrepresentation raises serious concerns about whether the entity is correctly identified, potentially leading to significant inaccuracies on my credit report. This issue directly violates 15 US Code 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ), which mandates that creditor information provided to Consumer Reporting Agencies ( CRAs ) must be accurate.

2. Missing Balance and Monthly Payment Information : My credit report reflects a balance of {$22000.00} as of XX/XX/XXXX, but it lacks detailed information about the payments leading to this balance. Specifically, the report does not mention the scheduled payments or explain how the balance correlates with the last payment date of XX/XX/XXXX. This discrepancy could constitute a billing error under 15 US Code 1666 ( b ) and may also violate 15 US Code 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ).

3. Incomplete Terms Duration : The Terms Duration is listed as NA, which is incomplete and complicates my understanding of the accounts terms. This omission violates 15 US Code 1681s-2 ( a ), as it reflects incomplete and potentially misleading information being reported to CRAs. 
4. Potential Inaccuracies in High-Balance Reporting : The high balance is reported as {$22000.00}, which exceeds the credit limit of {$20000.00}. However, there is no explanation provided regarding how this over-limit balance occurred or if any penalties were applied. Accurate reporting of such information is essential for compliance with 15 US Code 1681e ( b ). 
5. Inconsistent Reporting Dates : The account is reported as Charge off, but there are inconsistencies in the reported dates, including the " Date Opened : XX/XX/XXXX. '' These discrepancies suggest potential errors in reporting, which may violate 15 US Code 1681s-2 ( a ). Accurate reporting of the accounts dates is crucial, especially considering evidence that this account may have been transferred or sold.

6. Lack of Transparency Regarding Account Ownership : The account status indicates Charge off, but there is no clear information about when the charge-off occurred or whether the debt has been transferred to another lender or remains with the original creditor. Evidence I have obtained suggests
that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX either sold or assigned the account receivables to a debt collection agency in XX/XX/XXXX. This lack of transparency regarding the current ownership of the debt violates 15 US Code 1681g ( a ) ( 2 ), which requires CRAs to provide the full identifying information of any entity that has furnished consumer data. Without knowing who currently owns the debt, I am unable to properly address this dispute with the correct party.

Concern with CRAs Handling of the Dispute : I am particularly concerned with the CRAs handling of this dispute. The delay in resolving these issues is unacceptable and may constitute a violation of the FCRA.

Requested Resolution : I am requesting a thorough investigation into this account under both the FCRA and the FCBA. If the legal creditor can not verify the accuracy of the reported information, I demand that all incorrect entries be permanently removed from my credit report. CRAs must act promptly to investigate and correct any inaccuracies or unverifiable information.

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX Legal Basis for Dispute **15 USC 6801 Protection of Nonpublic Personal Information This section outlines the obligations of financial institutions to ensure that nonpublic personal information about consumers is protected. Specifically : 15 USC 6801 ( a ) states : It is the policy of the Congress that each financial institution has an affirmative and continuing obligation to respect the privacy of its customers and to protect the security and confidentiality of those customers nonpublic personal information.

In the context of charge-offs, financial institutions are required to manage consumer information in a manner that adheres to these privacy and security regulations. If information is shared or reported improperly, this can be seen as a violation of this privacy obligation. 

**15 USC 6802 Disclosure of Nonpublic Personal Information This section describes the circumstances under which a financial institution can disclose nonpublic personal information about consumers : 15 USC 6802 ( a ) states : Except as otherwise provided in this section, a financial institution may not, directly or through an affiliate, disclose to a nonaffiliated third party any nonpublic personal information about a consumer unless the consumer has been provided with a clear and conspicuous notice... and the consumer is given the opportunity to opt out of such disclosure. 
A charge-off may involve the sharing of nonpublic information that should be disclosed only under specific conditions, and without proper notice or consent, this constitutes a violation of the regulation. 

Request for Removal Based on these statutes, I request the immediate removal of the charge-off entries from my credit report. Specifically, these accounts were reported in a manner inconsistent with the privacy protection requirements outlined in the above statutes. 

These four accounts listed below are closed accounts that are adversely affecting my consumer report. According to 15 USC 1681 e b, they should be removed immediately. 

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX Legal Basis for Dispute **15 USC 1666b Timely Resolution of Credit Billing Disputes This statute requires that credit billing disputes be resolved in a timely manner and outlines the procedures creditors must follow. Specifically : 15 USC 1666b ( a ) states : A creditor shall acknowledge receipt of a notice of a billing error from a consumer within 30 days of receipt of such notice and shall, within two complete billing cycles or within 90 days, whichever is longer, correct the billing error or provide the consumer with a written explanation of why the creditor believes the billing error is not correct. 
If a creditor fails to adhere to these requirements, any negative information related to the disputed billing errors, including late payments, should not be reported on the consumers credit report. 

Dispute Reason The late payment entries reported on my credit report were related to a billing dispute where the creditor did not meet the legal requirements of 15 USC 1666b for resolving the dispute. Documentation of Authorization : Request that the creditor furnish evidence of your authorization for the inquiry. Communication Records : Request copies of any correspondence or communication between you and the creditor regarding the inquiry. I must bring to your attention that following my attempt to tender payment on the account in question, Capital One unilaterally closed my account without any prior notice or warning. I question how access to my own credit under the open-ended consumer credit plan, as defined in 15 U.S.C. 1602 ( g ), can be denied in such a manner. Moreover, Capital One has unjustly reported information to all three consumer reporting agencies without obtaining my written permissible purpose, in direct violation of the Fair Credit Reporting Act. 

Even if Capital One asserts that the terms and conditions permit such actions, I maintain that these terms are inherently fraudulent and deceptive due to the lack of proper disclosures that I never received under the Truth in Lending Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1605 ). Capital One has also failed to meet the requirements outlined in 15 U.S.C. 6801 and 6802, which protect my right to opt-out of having my information shared or reported to any third party. 

By engaging in these practices, Capital One N.A. has not only harmed me as a consumer but has also failed to respond to the correspondence I previously sent. This has subjected me to what can only be described as wage and debt slavery, as the bank has deceptively and intentionally misappropriated the meanings of critical terms such as " payment, '' " promise to pay, '' and " pay, '' as defined in Black 's Law Dictionary, 4th Edition. According to this legal authority, " payment '' simply refers to the fulfillment of an obligation.

Consumer complaint narrative:
What Happened : I have repeatedly sent payments to Discover for my account ending in XXXX via registered mail with XXXX, and XXXX has confirmed delivery to the address provided by XXXX. Despite this, XXXX continues to report my payments as late, which is inaccurate and in violation of my rights under the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ). I have contacted Discovers customer service multiple times, where I was given different addresses for payment submission, yet XXXX either claims they have not received the payments or does not acknowledge receipt. 

In addition to these issues, I am opting out of having my credit card utilization reported to the credit bureaus. Despite my right to opt out, as provided under relevant privacy laws, XXXX has continued to report this information without my consent. Furthermore, I do not receive a monthly privacy statement from XXXX, which is required to inform me of my rights and options regarding the reporting of my personal information. 

Applicable Laws : Discovers actions violate several federal laws and regulations : 15 U.S.C. 1681s2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) : This statute mandates that furnishers of information must report accurate information to credit reporting agencies. Discovers continued reporting of my payments as late, despite confirmation of payment receipt, is a clear violation.

15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ) : This requires credit reporting agencies to maintain reasonable procedures to ensure maximum possible accuracy in the information reported. Discovers failure to update the payment status accurately reflects non-compliance with this requirement.

12 CFR 1022.42 : This regulation demands accuracy in the information provided to consumer reporting agencies. Discovers inaccurate reporting of my payment status violates this regulation.

12 CFR Part 1016 ( Regulation P ) : This regulation governs the treatment of nonpublic personal information by financial institutions, requiring them to provide a privacy notice. XXXX has failed to provide me with a monthly privacy statement, which is required to allow me to opt out of certain types of information reporting. 
15 U.S.C. 6802 ( Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act ) : This law requires financial institutions to provide customers with a privacy notice that explains their information-sharing practices and allows customers to opt out of certain types of information sharing. XXXX has not provided me with the required privacy notices, nor have they honored my right to opt out of reporting my credit card utilization.

15 U.S.C. 1681n ( a ) : Under this statute, any entity that willfully fails to comply with the FCRA is liable for damages of at least {$1000.00} per violation. Discovers continuous misreporting of late payments, despite evidence of timely payment, and their failure to provide a privacy statement, constitute willful non-compliance.

Im sharing my story to help others understand the critical need for accurate credit reporting and the far-reaching consequences when mistakes go uncorrected. 

I am formally disputing significant errors on my credit report related to an account purportedly held with the Army and Air Force Exchange Service ( AAFES ). These errors involve discrepancies in the reported creditors name, inaccuracies in payment history, and violations of federal law, specifically under the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) and the Fair Credit Billing Act ( FCBA ). 

Key Issues : 1. Discrepancy in Creditor Name : The creditors name is inaccurately listed as ARMY & AIRFORCE EXCHANGE SERVI, which does not match the correct legal name, Army and Air Force Exchange Service. This misrepresentation raises serious concerns about whether the entity is correctly identified, potentially leading to significant inaccuracies on my credit report. This issue directly violates 15 US Code 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ), which mandates that creditor information provided to Consumer Reporting Agencies ( CRAs ) must be accurate. 

2. Inaccurate Payment Information : My credit report reflects a history of delinquencies that I believe are incorrectly reported. Specifically, the report lists a last payment date of XX/XX/XXXX, even though I have not made any payments since early XXXX. Moreover, unauthorized wage garnishments facilitated by the Defense Finance and Accounting Service ( DFAS ) have been wrongly applied to this account. These actions, coupled with the continued misreporting of payment information, constitute violations of the FCBA. 

3. Violation of Dispute Resolution Obligations : Despite multiple disputes I have filed, AAFES has failed to acknowledge or resolve these issues within the legally required timeframe as mandated by the FCBA. This failure has further impacted my credit standing. 

4. Misleading and False Representations : The continued reporting of inaccurate information regarding the high balance and past-due amounts on this account may violate the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ), particularly 15 U.S. Code 1692e, which prohibits the use of false or misleading representations in debt collection. 

5. Failure to Maintain Reasonable Procedures for Accuracy : The ongoing reporting of incorrect account names, inconsistent payment histories, and other inaccuracies suggests that the CRAs have not maintained reasonable procedures to ensure the highest possible accuracy in their reporting, as required by 15 US Code 1681e ( b ). 

I am requesting an immediate and thorough investigation into the accuracy of the information reported. If the legal creditor can not verify the accuracy of the reported information, I demand that all incorrect entries be permanently removed from my credit report. Additionally, I ask that all future communications regarding this dispute be sent to my designated mailing address. 

The accuracy and fairness of credit reporting are crucial to maintaining the integrity of our financial systems. The ongoing misreporting of information by AAFES and the CRAs has negatively affected my credit score and overall financial standing. This complaint aims to alert the CFPB and the FTC to these issues and seeks to ensure that all parties involved comply with federal laws to protect consumer rights. 

I authorize and direct ( 1 ) the consumer reporting agency identified in my complaint to share determinations of and actions taken by the company for the purpose of responding to my complaint, and ( 2 ) the CFPB to share this information with certain government agencies. The information provided is true to the best of my knowledge and belief. I understand that the CFPB can not act as my lawyer, a court of law, or a financial advisor.

The Privacy Act of 1974 is a federal law that protects individuals from the misuse of their personal information by the federal government. The act 's main goals are to balance the government 's need for information with the rights of individuals to privacy. 
The Privacy Act of 1974 : Protects individuals : The act protects individuals from the collection, use, maintenance, and disclosure of their personal information. 
Requires notice : Agencies must notify the public of their record systems. 
Requires consent : Agencies can not disclose an individual 's record without their written consent. 
Provides access : Individuals can request access to and changes to their records.

Establishes record-keeping requirements : The act sets forth requirements for how agencies keep records.

This misrepresentation is particularly concerning as it suggests that the entity listed on my credit report may be nonexistent or improperly identified, violating 15 US Code 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ). 2. Missing Balance and Monthly Payment Information : The credit report reflects a balance of {$0.00} as of XX/XX/year>, but does not provide detailed information about the payments leading to this balance, including the final payment date and amounts paid. I confirmed the validity of the text message by signing into my checking account and verifying that an unauthorized transaction for {$430.00} was listed in my Account Summary. I replied " N '' to the text message, and Wells Fargo responded by asking me to call them. After my text reply, I noticed that the {$430.00} was immediately credited in my account. I noticed no other unauthorized activity at that time.

I called the number, and the customer service representative asked me about two additional transactions that were made immediately after the unauthorized {$430.00} transaction : 1. A tele-transfer transaction that transfered {$3200.00} from my savings account to my checking account ( attached ; note that the transaction is dated XX/XX/XXXX, but actually occurred XX/XX/XXXX. I believe the discrepancy is due to the item being moved to my new checking account ) XXXX. A {$5700.00} transaction made using my debit card for DraftKings ( attached ) I informed the representative that both of those transactions were unauthorized. 

The representative stated that it appeared my accounts were compromised and strongly recommended closing my savings and checking accounts and canceling my debit card. I agreed, and then worked with the representative to file fraud claims for the unauthorized tele-transfer and the unauthorized {$5700.00} XXXX transaction. 

I next received two letters from Wells Fargo dated XX/XX/XXXX informing me that my claims had been closed ( see attached ) : XXXX. The claim for the tele-transfer was closed because the money was moved from one of my accounts to another, and therefore no funds were actually lost during the tele-transfer transaction. 

XXXX. The claim for the {$5700.00} unauthorized XXXX transaction was closed because, according to Wells Fargo, " we have determined the transaction was authorized or that a processing error did not occur. '' It is important to note that the XXXX website is geo-blocked in the State of Idaho where I reside ( see attached screenshot from XXXX XXXX XXXX  ). I can prove that I was in Idaho on XX/XX/XXXX because I took an international flight from the XXXX XXXX ( see attached ) a couple of hours after filing the fraud claims with Wells Fargo. 

Because Wells Fargo suspected my debit card may have been comprised as a result of the initial text message I received on XX/XX/XXXX, that two additional transactions occured immediately after that unauthorized {$430.00} transaction, that Wells Fargo suspected fraud had occurred such that they strongly encouraged me to closed my accounts, and that the DraftKings website is geo-blocked in the State of Idaho, XXXX believe my fraud claim for {$5700.00} was closed in error. 

No one other than myself was authorized to use my debit card. My debit card was not lost, and my phone was in my possession at all times. 

I am asking to CFPB to discuss this matter with Wells Fargo on my behalf.

These inaccuracies have negatively impacted my credit score and overall financial standing. The issues I am raising are of serious concern regarding compliance with the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) and the Fair Credit Billing Act ( FCBA ).

Key Issues : 1. Discrepancy in Creditor Name : The creditors name is inaccurately listed as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, which may not match the correct legal name of the entity. This misrepresentation raises serious concerns about whether the entity is correctly identified, potentially leading to significant inaccuracies on my credit report. This issue directly violates 15 US Code 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ), which mandates that creditor information provided to Consumer Reporting Agencies ( CRAs ) must be accurate.

2. Missing Balance and Monthly Payment Information : My credit report reflects a balance of {$1900.00} as of XX/XX/XXXX, but it lacks detailed information about the payments leading to this balance. Specifically, the report does not mention the scheduled payments or explain how the balance correlates with the last payment date of XX/XX/XXXX. This discrepancy could constitute a billing error under 15 US Code 1666 ( b ) and may also violate 15 US Code 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ).

3. Incomplete Terms Duration : The Terms Duration is listed as NA, which is incomplete and complicates my understanding of the accounts terms. This omission violates 15 US Code 1681s-2 ( a ), as it reflects incomplete and potentially misleading information being reported to CRAs.

Secondly, reporting charged-off accounts as still collectible or owed is not only fraudulent and dishonest but also constitutes an illegal attempt at double recovery. 
The legal principle prohibiting double recovery is well-established in case law, as evidenced by the following precedents : XXXX XXXX  XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ) : The U.S. Supreme Court established that a taxpayer must recognize income when a debt is discharged, preventing them from benefitting from both a deduction and a continued claim on the debt. 

XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX  XXXX, XXXX XXXX. XXXX ( XXXX ) : The Tax Court highlighted the importance of substantiating a bad debt deduction, ruling that once a debt is claimed as uncollectible, it can not be treated as still owed. 

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  XXXX, XXXX XXXX. XXXX ( XXXX ) : The Tax Court emphasized that a taxpayer can not claim a deduction for a bad debt while simultaneously asserting the debt 's collectability, thereby avoiding double recovery.

Rev. Rul. 70-367, 1970-2 C.B. 37 : The IRS clearly stated that once a bad debt deduction is taken, the debt is considered worthless, and the taxpayer can not later attempt to collect on it.

Consumer complaint narrative:
XXXX XXXX XXXX Ally Bank is negligent of not investigating previously canceled recurring XXXX transfers that reappear several months after they were canceled and result in unauthorized attempts to make withdrawals from customers accounts. In addition, Ally Banks record keeping practices regarding customers requests to schedule, modify, and cancel recurring XXXX transfers are weak as they allow deletion of the information. 

Dear CFPB, I am writing to express my deep concern regarding an attempt of Ally Bank to transfer funds in amount of {$2700.00} from my checking account on XX/XX/XXXX, which Ally Bank claims were part of a recurring monthly XXXX transfer. This incident is troubling given the fact that I had explicitly canceled the entire recurring transfer series in question on XX/XX/XXXX. 

On XX/XX/XXXX I had scheduled a recurring monthly XXXX transfer in the amount of {$2700.00} from my checking account ending in XXXX to one of my XXXX recipients XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ) at XXXX with the initial transfer anticipated to occur on XX/XX/XXXX and then on the XXXX of every subsequent month ( XX/XX/XXXX, XX/XX/XXXX, etc ). However, subsequently I canceled the entire series of the recurring transfers on XX/XX/XXXX. In addition, in XX/XX/XXXX, I canceled absolutely all remaining ( I had at least three other recurring XXXX transfers with Ally Bank at that time ) recurring transfers associated with my account. At the end of XX/XX/XXXX I also verified through my online banking that no outstanding future scheduled XXXX transfers were showing up on my account. 

Despite these clear cancellations, there was an unexpected attempt to make a XXXX transfer from my account on XX/XX/XXXX for the amount matching the previously canceled recurring transfer. When I contacted Ally Bank and learned that my account was blocked due to not enough funds to cover the transfer I informed Ally Bank that the transfer attempt was clearly a banks error since I had canceled all recurring transfers months prior. The Ally Banks representative I was conversing with acknowledged the cancellation I had made in XXXX and indicated that they would file a report ( case number XXXX ) so that Ally Bank would investigate the matter. 

However, my subsequent inquiries about the status of this investigation have yielded unsatisfactory results. The bank has informed me that they can not locate a record of my earlier cancellation, despite my clear recollection and previous correspondence. Ally Bank was using the cancellations that were processed on or after XX/XX/XXXX ( those that were done after the fact to correct the problem that had already occurred ) as an excuse not to investigate the issue. The text of the original report that Ally Banks representative had filed as case number XXXX also can not be located by the banks representatives. The bank had claimed that no cancellations of the recurring transfer had occurred ( according to the records that they have ) prior to XX/XX/XXXX. 
It is important to note that if the recurring transfer had not been canceled prior to XX/XX/XXXX, it would have been expected to be processed on XX/XX/XXXX, XX/XX/XXXX, and XX/XX/XXXX. The fact that no such transfers occurred during these periods strongly suggests that a cancellation was indeed in place. The attached correspondence with Ally Bank shows that they are aware that a cancellation of the recurring transfer originally scheduled for XX/XX/XXXX has happened on XX/XX/XXXX, however, to my additional questions whether, according to the Ally Banks records, that cancellation was for the entire recurring sequence of transfers or not Ally Bank has not responded. 

In one of the conversations I had with Ally Bank on XX/XX/XXXX I asked Ally Banks representatives to check the history of the email communications that Ally Bank had with me with regards to my account activities. Such correspondence history should have included all confirmations of my XXXX transfers cancellation requests and would help Ally Bank to identify using their internal data on what dates my recurring transfer sequence cancellation requests had occurred. Ally Banks representative informed that they do not have access to the history of the email communications prior to XX/XX/XXXX. During that conversation I had made a request for reasonable accommodations under the Americans with Disabilities Act to Ally Bank to restore my email communications with Ally Bank since XX/XX/XXXX ( request reference number XXXX ). In the attached document I am enclosing Ally Banks Executive Customer Relations representatives response to my request claiming that Ally Bank can not accommodate it and not providing any explanation of whether granting me the requested reasonable accommodation would constitute an undue burden on the bank or would require the bank to fundamentally alter the nature of the service it provides to the public. 

I believe that the described incident of Ally Banks attempting to perform a transfer that was canceled by the customer months prior and the banks inability to properly investigate the cause of that is indicative of a serious flaw in Ally Bank 's or its vendor 's system, which is allowing unauthorized transfer attempts to occur. Furthermore, the bank 's failure to investigate this issue thoroughly and its apparent deletion of relevant requests history demonstrate the Banks lack of due diligence. 

Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter.

Communication Records : Request copies of any correspondence or communication between you and the creditor regarding the inquiry. This may include emails, letters, or notes documenting your interactions with the creditor.

Continuously reporting this charge-off as a new event each month does not reset the statute of limitations and is improper. 

I request that you promptly investigate this account and correct the inaccurate information by removing the repeated entries of the charge-off from my payment history. Please update my credit report accordingly and provide me with a confirmation of these corrections. 

Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter.

I am filing this complaint, hoping to get your help looking into this matter, in which I feel my rights have been violated. 

I want to report apparent illegal activities by a hospital and debt collection agency committed in relation to my medical debt. On XX/XX/XXXX, I had an XXXX XXXX done by XXXX XXXX XXXX, which is part of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The first and only bill I received was dated XX/XX/XXXX. That bill did not have a specific due date. For a due date, the bill only says, UPON RECEIPT. At the time I was disputing the amount which my insurance paid, hoping they would pay more. On XX/XX/XXXX, we received a bill from Creditors Bureau USA, dated XX/XX/year>. The Bill says that Between XXXX and today, interest had been charged. This is preposterous. There is no clear disclosure when interest began to be charged. The bill makes it seem that interest began accruing the day of the medical procedure. 

First, according to California law, Hospitals can not sell your patient debt to a debt buyer unless you are ineligible for financial assistance, or you have not responded to a hospitals attempt to offer assistance for 180 days. We were never offered any such assistance or given 180 days to resolve this bill. My debt was sold to a debt collector less than 180 ( around 60 days with no due date ) after the first bill was received, let alone, it was only 149 days since my procedure. I am not sure if this violates any federal laws. 

Second, in its first written communication with us, Creditors Bureau USA did not inform me of a timeframe for reporting negative information, which is required by California law. 

Third, according to California law, Hospitals are required to provide you with a specific notice before transferring a hospital debt to a debt collector. This notice will include a copy of an application for free or reduced care under that hospitals policy. In the first written communication with you, debt collectors must also send you a copy of this notice. XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX failed to provide me with specific notice that the debt was being transferred to a debt collector, violating my rights. Not only was I not told by the original creditor that the debt was being transferred, only two months after the initial bill, but I was not given a copy for free or reduced care, which is my right. Finally, the debt collector did not send me a copy of this notice either in their first communication with me. While I am still working with insurance, my debt gets sent to a debt agency. This is unfair and illegal. 

Lastly, debt collectors may collect interest, fees, charges, or other expenses to your debt only if they are expressly authorized by the agreement creating the debt or are otherwise permitted by law. There was never any agreement with the hospital to pay interest. Nowhere in the original bill does it say anything about charging interest. How can Creditors Bureau USA begin charging interest on a bill, which never said anything about interest, and have it backdated to the day of the procedure?

I have requested the original contract over a three year period and have never received it per 15 US CODE 1692 ( G ), also known as the Validation of Debts section, is part of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act and Title 15 of the U.S. Code, Commerce and Trade. It requires debt collectors to follow certain procedures when communicating with consumers about debt collection : Validation notice Within five days of the initial communication, debt collectors must send consumers a written notice that includes the amount of the debt, the creditor 's name, and a statement that the debt will be considered valid if the consumer doesn't dispute it within 30 days. The notice must also state that the debt collector will provide the consumer with the original creditor 's name and address if requested within 30 days. 
Disputed debts If the consumer disputes the debt, the debt collector must stop collection efforts and : Obtain verification of the debt or a copy of a judgment Mail the verification or judgment to the consumer Other provisions Debt collectors are also prohibited from taking certain actions, such as : Threatening or taking non-judicial action to disable or dispossess property if there is no right to possession, no intention to take possession, or the property is exempt by law Using unfair or unconscionable means to collect a debt, such as collecting amounts that aren't authorized by the agreement creating the debt or permitted by law

12 CFR 1016.7 Form of opt out notice to consumers ; opt out methods. ( a ) ( 1 ) Form of opt out notice. If you are required to provide an opt out notice under 1016.10 ( a ), you must provide a clear and conspicuous notice to each of your consumers that accurately explains the right to opt out under that section. The notice must state : ( i ) That you disclose or reserve the right to disclose nonpublic personal information about your consumer to a nonaffiliated third party ; ( ii ) That the consumer has the right to opt out of that disclosure; and ( iii ) A reasonable means by which the consumer may exercise the opt out right. ( 2 ) Examples ( i ) Adequate opt out notice. You provide adequate notice that the consumer can opt out of the disclosure of nonpublic personal information to a nonaffiliated third party if you : ( A ) Identify all of the categories of nonpublic personal information that you disclose or reserve the right to disclose, and all of the categories of nonaffiliated third parties to which you disclose the information, as described in 1016.6 ( a ) ( 2 ) and ( 3 ) of this part, and state that the consumer can opt out of the disclosure of that information; and ( B ) Identify the financial products or services that the consumer obtains from you, either singly or jointly, to which the opt out direction would apply. ( ii ) Reasonable opt out means. You provide a reasonable means to exercise an opt out right if you : ( A ) Designate check-off boxes in a prominent position on the relevant forms with the opt out notice ; ( B ) Include a reply form together with the opt out notice that, in the case of financial institutions described in 1016.3 ( l ) ( 3 ) of this part, includes the address to which the form should be mailed ; ( C ) Provide an electronic means to opt out, such as a form that can be sent via electronic mail or a process at your Web site, if the consumer agrees to the electronic delivery of information ; or ( D ) Provide a toll-free telephone number that consumers may call to opt out. ( iii ) Unreasonable opt out means. You do not provide a reasonable means of opting out if : ( A ) The only means of opting out is for the consumer to write his or her own letter to exercise that opt out right; or ( B ) The only means of opting out as described in any notice subsequent to the initial notice is to use a check-off box that you provided with the initial notice but did not include with the subsequent notice. ( iv ) Specific opt out means. You may require each consumer to opt out through a specific means, as long as that means is reasonable for that consumer. ( b ) Same form as initial notice permitted. You may provide the opt out notice together with or on the same written or electronic form as the initial notice you provide in accordance with 1016.4. ( c ) Initial notice required when opt out notice delivered subsequent to initial notice. If you provide the opt out notice later than required for the initial notice in accordance with 1016.4 of this part, you must also include a copy of the initial notice with the opt out notice in writing or, if the consumer agrees, electronically.

15 U.S. Code 1692e - False or misleading representations A debt collector may not use any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt. Without limiting the general application of the foregoing, the following conduct is a violation of this section : ( 1 ) The false representation or implication that the debt collector is vouched for, bonded by, or affiliated with the United States or any State, including the use of any badge, uniform, or facsimile thereof.

( 2 ) The false representation of ( A ) the character, amount, or legal status of any debt; or ( B ) any services rendered or compensation which may be lawfully received by any debt collector for the collection of a debt.

( 3 ) The false representation or implication that any individual is an attorney or that any communication is from an attorney.

( 4 ) The representation or implication that nonpayment of any debt will result in the arrest or imprisonment of any person or the seizure, garnishment, attachment, or sale of any property or wages of any person unless such action is lawful and the debt collector or creditor intends to take such action.

( 5 ) The threat to take any action that can not legally be taken or that is not intended to be taken.

( 6 ) The false representation or implication that a sale, referral, or other transfer of any interest in a debt shall cause the consumer to ( A ) lose any claim or defense to payment of the debt; or ( B ) become subject to any practice prohibited by this subchapter.

( 7 ) The false representation or implication that the consumer committed any crime or other conduct in order to disgrace the consumer.

( 8 ) Communicating or threatening to communicate to any person credit information which is known or which should be known to be false, including the failure to communicate that a disputed debt is disputed.

( 9 ) The use or distribution of any written communication which simulates or is falsely represented to be a document authorized, issued, or approved by any court, official, or agency of the United States or any State, or which creates a false impression as to its source, authorization, or approval.

( 10 ) The use of any false representation or deceptive means to collect or attempt to collect any debt or to obtain information concerning a consumer.

( 11 ) The failure to disclose in the initial written communication with the consumer and, in addition, if the initial communication with the consumer is oral, in that initial oral communication, that the debt collector is attempting to collect a debt and that any information obtained will be used for that purpose, and the failure to disclose in subsequent communications that the communication is from a debt collector, except that this paragraph shall not apply to a formal pleading made in connection with a legal action.

( 12 ) The false representation or implication that accounts have been turned over to innocent purchasers for value.

( 13 ) The false representation or implication that documents are legal process.

( 14 ) The use of any business, company, or organization name other than the true name of the debt collectors business, company, or organization.

( 15 ) The false representation or implication that documents are not legal process forms or do not require action by the consumer.

( 16 ) The false representation or implication that a debt collector operates or is employed by a consumer reporting agency as defined by section 1681a ( f ) of this title.

15 U.S. Code 1692f - Unfair practices A debt collector may not use unfair or unconscionable means to collect or attempt to collect any debt. Without limiting the general application of the foregoing, the following conduct is a violation of this section : ( 1 ) The collection of any amount ( including any interest, fee, charge, or expense incidental to the principal obligation ) unless such amount is expressly authorized by the agreement creating the debt or permitted by law.

( 2 ) The acceptance by a debt collector from any person of a check or other payment instrument postdated by more than five days unless such person is notified in writing of the debt collectors intent to deposit such check or instrument not more than ten nor less than three business days prior to such deposit.

( 3 ) The solicitation by a debt collector of any postdated check or other postdated payment instrument for the purpose of threatening or instituting criminal prosecution.

( 4 ) Depositing or threatening to deposit any postdated check or other postdated payment instrument prior to the date on such check or instrument.

( 5 ) Causing charges to be made to any person for communications by concealment of the true purpose of the communication. Such charges include, but are not limited to, collect telephone calls and telegram fees.

( 6 ) Taking or threatening to take any nonjudicial action to effect dispossession or disablement of property if ( A ) there is no present right to possession of the property claimed as collateral through an enforceable security interest ; ( B ) there is no present intention to take possession of the property ; or ( C ) the property is exempt by law from such dispossession or disablement.

( 7 ) Communicating with a consumer regarding a debt by post card.

( 8 ) Using any language or symbol, other than the debt collectors address, on any envelope when communicating with a consumer by use of the mails or by telegram, except that a debt collector may use his business name if such name does not indicate that he is in the debt collection business.

12 CFR 1026.11 - Treatment of credit balances ; account termination.

( a ) Credit balances. When a credit balance in excess of {$1.00} is created on a credit account ( through transmittal of funds to a creditor in excess of the total balance due on an account, through rebates of unearned finance charges or insurance premiums, or through amounts otherwise owed to or held for the benefit of the consumer ), the creditor shall : ( 1 ) Credit the amount of the credit balance to the consumer 's account ; ( 2 ) Refund any part of the remaining credit balance within seven business days from receipt of a written request from the consumer ; ( 3 ) Make a good faith effort to refund to the consumer by cash, check, or money order, or credit to a deposit account of the consumer, any part of the credit balance remaining in the account for more than six months. No further action is required if the consumer 's current location is not known to the creditor and can not be traced through the consumer 's last known address or telephone number.

( b ) Account termination.

( 1 ) A creditor shall not terminate an account prior to its expiration date solely because the consumer does not incur a finance charge.

( 2 ) Nothing in paragraph ( b ) ( 1 ) of this section prohibits a creditor from terminating an account that is inactive for three or more consecutive months. An account is inactive for purposes of this paragraph if no credit has been extended ( such as by purchase, cash advance or balance transfer ) and if the account has no outstanding balance.

( c ) Timely settlement of estate debts ( 1 ) General rule.

( i ) Reasonable policies and procedures required. For credit card accounts under an open-end ( not home-secured ) consumer credit plan, card issuers must adopt reasonable written policies and procedures designed to ensure that an administrator of an estate of a deceased accountholder can determine the amount of and pay any balance on the account in a timely manner.

( ii ) Application to joint accounts. Paragraph ( c ) of this section does not apply to the account of a deceased consumer if a joint accountholder remains on the account.

( 2 ) Timely statement of balance ( i ) Requirement. Upon request by the administrator of an estate, a card issuer must provide the administrator with the amount of the balance on a deceased consumer 's account in a timely manner.

( ii ) Safe harbor. For purposes of paragraph ( c ) ( 2 ) ( i ) of this section, providing the amount of the balance on the account within 30 days of receiving the request is deemed to be timely.

( 3 ) Limitations after receipt of request from administrator ( i ) Limitation on fees and increases in annual percentage rates. After receiving a request from the administrator of an estate for the amount of the balance on a deceased consumer 's account, a card issuer must not impose any fees on the account ( such as a late fee, annual fee, or over-the-limit fee ) or increase any annual percentage rate, except as provided by 1026.55 ( b ) ( 2 ).

( ii ) Limitation on trailing or residual interest. A card issuer must waive or rebate any additional finance charge due to a periodic interest rate if payment in full of the balance disclosed pursuant to paragraph ( c ) ( 2 ) of this section is received within 30 days after disclosure.

12 CFR 1016.7 Form of opt out notice to consumers ; opt out methods.

( a ) ( 1 ) Form of opt out notice. If you are required to provide an opt out notice under 1016.10 ( a ), you must provide a clear and conspicuous notice to each of your consumers that accurately explains the right to opt out under that section. The notice must state : ( i ) That you disclose or reserve the right to disclose nonpublic personal information about your consumer to a nonaffiliated third party ; ( ii ) That the consumer has the right to opt out of that disclosure; and ( iii ) A reasonable means by which the consumer may exercise the opt out right.

( 2 ) Examples ( i ) Adequate opt out notice. You provide adequate notice that the consumer can opt out of the disclosure of nonpublic personal information to a nonaffiliated third party if you : ( A ) Identify all of the categories of nonpublic personal information that you disclose or reserve the right to disclose, and all of the categories of nonaffiliated third parties to which you disclose the information, as described in 1016.6 ( a ) ( 2 ) and ( 3 ) of this part, and state that the consumer can opt out of the disclosure of that information; and ( B ) Identify the financial products or services that the consumer obtains from you, either singly or jointly, to which the opt out direction would apply.

( ii ) Reasonable opt out means. You provide a reasonable means to exercise an opt out right if you : ( A ) Designate check-off boxes in a prominent position on the relevant forms with the opt out notice ; ( B ) Include a reply form together with the opt out notice that, in the case of financial institutions described in 1016.3 ( l ) ( 3 ) of this part, includes the address to which the form should be mailed ; ( C ) Provide an electronic means to opt out, such as a form that can be sent via electronic mail or a process at your Web site, if the consumer agrees to the electronic delivery of information ; or ( D ) Provide a toll-free telephone number that consumers may call to opt out.

( iii ) Unreasonable opt out means. You do not provide a reasonable means of opting out if : ( A ) The only means of opting out is for the consumer to write his or her own letter to exercise that opt out right; or ( B ) The only means of opting out as described in any notice subsequent to the initial notice is to use a check-off box that you provided with the initial notice but did not include with the subsequent notice.

( iv ) Specific opt out means. You may require each consumer to opt out through a specific means, as long as that means is reasonable for that consumer.

( b ) Same form as initial notice permitted. You may provide the opt out notice together with or on the same written or electronic form as the initial notice you provide in accordance with 1016.4.

( c ) Initial notice required when opt out notice delivered subsequent to initial notice. If you provide the opt out notice later than required for the initial notice in accordance with 1016.4 of this part, you must also include a copy of the initial notice with the opt out notice in writing or, if the consumer agrees, electronically.

15 U.S. Code 1692e - False or misleading representations A debt collector may not use any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt. Without limiting the general application of the foregoing, the following conduct is a violation of this section : ( 1 ) The false representation or implication that the debt collector is vouched for, bonded by, or affiliated with the United States or any State, including the use of any badge, uniform, or facsimile thereof.

( 2 ) The false representation of ( A ) the character, amount, or legal status of any debt; or ( B ) any services rendered or compensation which may be lawfully received by any debt collector for the collection of a debt.

( 3 ) The false representation or implication that any individual is an attorney or that any communication is from an attorney.

( 4 ) The representation or implication that nonpayment of any debt will result in the arrest or imprisonment of any person or the seizure, garnishment, attachment, or sale of any property or wages of any person unless such action is lawful and the debt collector or creditor intends to take such action.

( 5 ) The threat to take any action that can not legally be taken or that is not intended to be taken.

( 6 ) The false representation or implication that a sale, referral, or other transfer of any interest in a debt shall cause the consumer to ( A ) lose any claim or defense to payment of the debt; or ( B ) become subject to any practice prohibited by this subchapter.

( 7 ) The false representation or implication that the consumer committed any crime or other conduct in order to disgrace the consumer.

( 8 ) Communicating or threatening to communicate to any person credit information which is known or which should be known to be false, including the failure to communicate that a disputed debt is disputed.

( 9 ) The use or distribution of any written communication which simulates or is falsely represented to be a document authorized, issued, or approved by any court, official, or agency of the United States or any State, or which creates a false impression as to its source, authorization, or approval.

( 10 ) The use of any false representation or deceptive means to collect or attempt to collect any debt or to obtain information concerning a consumer.

( 11 ) The failure to disclose in the initial written communication with the consumer and, in addition, if the initial communication with the consumer is oral, in that initial oral communication, that the debt collector is attempting to collect a debt and that any information obtained will be used for that purpose, and the failure to disclose in subsequent communications that the communication is from a debt collector, except that this paragraph shall not apply to a formal pleading made in connection with a legal action.

( 12 ) The false representation or implication that accounts have been turned over to innocent purchasers for value.

12 CFR 1026.11 - Treatment of credit balances ; account termination.

( a ) Credit balances. When a credit balance in excess of {$1.00} is created on a credit account ( through transmittal of funds to a creditor in excess of the total balance due on an account, through rebates of unearned finance charges or insurance premiums, or through amounts otherwise owed to or held for the benefit of the consumer ), the creditor shall : ( 1 ) Credit the amount of the credit balance to the consumer 's account ; ( 2 ) Refund any part of the remaining credit balance within seven business days from receipt of a written request from the consumer ; ( 3 ) Make a good faith effort to refund to the consumer by cash, check, or money order, or credit to a deposit account of the consumer, any part of the credit balance remaining in the account for more than six months. No further action is required if the consumer 's current location is not known to the creditor and can not be traced through the consumer 's last known address or telephone number.

( b ) Account termination.

( 1 ) A creditor shall not terminate an account prior to its expiration date solely because the consumer does not incur a finance charge.

( 2 ) Nothing in paragraph ( b ) ( 1 ) of this section prohibits a creditor from terminating an account that is inactive for three or more consecutive months. An account is inactive for purposes of this paragraph if no credit has been extended ( such as by purchase, cash advance or balance transfer ) and if the account has no outstanding balance.

( c ) Timely settlement of estate debts ( 1 ) General rule.

( i ) Reasonable policies and procedures required. For credit card accounts under an open-end ( not home-secured ) consumer credit plan, card issuers must adopt reasonable written policies and procedures designed to ensure that an administrator of an estate of a deceased accountholder can determine the amount of and pay any balance on the account in a timely manner.

( ii ) Application to joint accounts. Paragraph ( c ) of this section does not apply to the account of a deceased consumer if a joint accountholder remains on the account.

( 2 ) Timely statement of balance ( i ) Requirement. Upon request by the administrator of an estate, a card issuer must provide the administrator with the amount of the balance on a deceased consumer 's account in a timely manner.

( ii ) Safe harbor. For purposes of paragraph ( c ) ( 2 ) ( i ) of this section, providing the amount of the balance on the account within 30 days of receiving the request is deemed to be timely.

( 3 ) Limitations after receipt of request from administrator ( i ) Limitation on fees and increases in annual percentage rates. After receiving a request from the administrator of an estate for the amount of the balance on a deceased consumer 's account, a card issuer must not impose any fees on the account ( such as a late fee, annual fee, or over-the-limit fee ) or increase any annual percentage rate, except as provided by 1026.55 ( b ) ( 2 ).

( ii ) Limitation on trailing or residual interest. A card issuer must waive or rebate any additional finance charge due to a periodic interest rate if payment in full of the balance disclosed pursuant to paragraph ( c ) ( 2 ) of this section is received within 30 days after disclosure.

Consumer complaint narrative:
On XX/XX/year>, I received an offer from American Express ( AMEX ) inviting me to apply for " The Blue Business Cash Card '' via phone or their website. In response to this offer, I contacted AMEX by telephone to proceed with the application. During this call, I was instructed to provide all necessary information for the application, including my business name, Employer Identification Number ( EIN ), business address, as well as my personal identifying information. As requested by AMEX, I provided consideration, my full name, Social Security Number ( SSN ), and Date of Birth. 

Upon receipt of this information, the AMEX representative acknowledged the submission but subsequently informed me that, based on their assessment, I was deemed more suitable for the Gold Business Card rather than the Blue Business Cash Card. Consequently, the representative submitted an application for the Gold Business Card. 

Following the submission, I was informed that AMEX had declined my application. I immediately objected, asserting that AMEX 's solicitation specifically offered the Blue Business Cash Card without any indication that my eligibility was contingent upon qualifying for an alternative product. I further contended that AMEX has a legal obligation to fulfill the initial offer upon the receipt of all required information. 

Moreover, I expressed concern that during this transaction, I provided sensitive personal and business information, which holds significant value, based on AMEX 's offer. This information could have been securitized without my authorization. I also noted that an active fraud alert is on my account due to prior identity theft, which should have prompted AMEX to verify the information, as mandated by the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ). AMEX failed to verify the information despite the active fraud alert. 

By law, I am entitled to the fulfillment of the original offer presented to me. As the beneficial owner, I seek to retain all interest and proceeds, whether expressly stated or implied. Despite my objections, the representative indicated that no recourse was available. Reference # XXXX I am fully prepared to advance this matter. I have reviewed the AMEX Indenture Agreement, as well as Form XXXX and Form XXXX filings, which provide substantial evidence supporting my claims. Additionally, I have consulted various other relevant sources. 

An offer by law Offer is part of contract negotiations where a party agrees to do or not do something in exchange for consideration. An offer must be stated and delivered in a way that would lead a reasonable person to expect a binding contract to arise from its acceptance. An offer gives the offeree the ability to accept and form an enforceable contract. 

When a valid offer is made, an acceptance by the offeree creates a binding contract. An offeror generally can not retract the offer once the other party has accepted. A court may not find a binding contract regardless, though, if the negotiation did not involve consideration, involves an illusory promise, or if the offeror did not have the capacity to enter into the contract. However, a contract offer can be withdrawn by notification to the offeree of the intent to withdraw the offer before the offeree has accepted. Offerors typically can withdraw an offer before acceptance in any contract negotiation unless the parties have created an enforceable option contract. If the offeree rejects the offer, the offer can no longer be accepted by the offeree. 

An offer can also be made in the form of a counteroffer. The offeree that receives the initial offer can make a new offer of their own instead of accepting the initial offer. This counteroffer acts as a rejection of the initial offer and creates an entirely new offer that can be accepted or rejected. 

Consideration is a promise, performance, or forbearance bargained by a promisor in exchange for their promise. Consideration is the main element of a contract. Without consideration by both parties, a contract can not be enforceable. For instance, if a person used the money to purchase an apple, the apple is the merchants consideration, and the money is the persons consideration. 

Types : Consideration could be a promise, performance, forbearance, or property with legal value, but the economic benefit is not required. 
A gift or gratuitous promise can not be a consideration for they have no bargaining. The past performance also can not be a consideration as there is no exchange. 

Substitute for consideration : A contract without consideration could be enforceable if it has a substitute. Substitutes are promissory estoppel or detrimental reliance under Restatement ( Second ) of Contracts, or good faith modification under UCC. 
Promissory estoppel/detrimental reliance : A contract without consideration is enforceable if the nonperformance of the promisor will cause injustice. Elements of promissory estoppel are ( i ) the promise has reasonable, foreseeable, and detrimental reliance on the promisor, and ( ii ) the enforcement of the promise is necessary to avoid injustice. 
Good faith modification : A modified contract is a kind of new agreement, which changes parties obligations and then requires new consideration. But contract modification made in good faith under UCC is enforceable even without consideration

Since XX/XX/XXXX, I have been in contact with Fortiva regarding discrepancies in my credit report. The Privacy Act of 1974 is a federal law that protects individuals from the misuse of their personal information by the federal government. The act 's main goals are to balance the government 's need for information with the rights of individuals to privacy. 
The Privacy Act of 1974 : Protects individuals : The act protects individuals from the collection, use, maintenance, and disclosure of their personal information. 
Requires notice : Agencies must notify the public of their record systems. 
Requires consent : Agencies can not disclose an individual 's record without their written consent. 
Provides access : Individuals can request access to and changes to their records. 
Establishes record-keeping requirements : The act sets forth requirements for how agencies keep records.

Charge of accounts are considered, certificates of indebtedness, pursuant to I.R.S publication XXXX and it is now considered income and income can not be reporting on my consumer credit report, pursuant to Privacy act of 1974. 
The Privacy Act of 1974 is a federal law that protects individuals from the misuse of their personal information by the federal government. The act 's main goals are to balance the government 's need for information with the rights of individuals to privacy. 
The Privacy Act of 1974 : Protects individuals : The act protects individuals from the collection, use, maintenance, and disclosure of their personal information. 
Requires notice : Agencies must notify the public of their record systems. 
Requires consent : Agencies can not disclose an individual 's record without their written consent. 
Provides access : Individuals can request access to and changes to their records. 
Establishes record-keeping requirements : The act sets forth requirements for how agencies keep records.

Subject : Complaint Against PNC Bank for Violating the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) - Refusal to Process Credit Application Unless Consumer Waived Right to Opt-Out of Data Sharing Date of Incident : XX/XX/year> Bank Name : PNC Bank Location : Online/ via phone To Whom It May Concern : I am filing this complaint against PNC Bank for actions that I believe are in violation of the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), specifically concerning my right to opt-out of data sharing for account review purposes. 

Incident Details : On XX/XX/year>, I applied for a personal line of credit with PNC Bank. During the application process, I was presented with credit disclosures that included a request for my consent to share my payment history with Credit Reporting Agencies ( CRAs ) for account review purposes.

I informed the bank representative that I did not consent to having my payment history shared with CRAs. Despite exercising my right to opt-out under the FCRA, PNC Bank refused to proceed with my credit application unless I agreed to allow my payment history to be shared.

Applicable Law : Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1681 et seq. ), consumers have the right to opt-out of having their credit information shared with third parties for account review purposes. Specifically : 15 U.S.C. 1681b ( a
) ( 3 ) ( F ) provides that consumer reporting agencies may furnish a consumer report to a person which " has a legitimate business need for the information ... in connection with a business transaction that is initiated by the consumer. '' 15 U.S.C. 1681b ( c ) ( 1 ) allows consumers to opt-out of having their information shared for certain prescreened offers of credit or insurance. 
Additionally, the FCRA prohibits creditors from making the extension of credit conditional on the waiver of the consumers right to opt-out. Conditioning the approval of my credit application on my consent to share my payment history constitutes a violation of my rights under the FCRA. 
Complaint : I believe that PNC Banks refusal to process my credit application unless I waived my right to opt-out of data sharing with CRAs for account review purposes is a violation of the FCRA. By making the extension of credit contingent on the waiver of my rights, PNC Bank has engaged in practices that are not only unfair but also illegal under federal law. 

Requested Resolution : I request that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau : Investigate PNC Banks practices regarding conditioning credit applications on the waiver of FCRA opt-out rights. 
Ensure that PNC Bank ceases such practices immediately and takes corrective action to comply with the FCRA. 
Take appropriate enforcement action against PNC Bank for this violation. 
Inform me of any steps I need to take to ensure my rights are protected and that my credit application is processed fairly. 
I appreciate your attention to this serious matter and look forward to your prompt response.

( a ) Credit balances. When a credit balance in excess of {$1.00} is created on a credit account ( through transmittal of funds to a creditor in excess of the total balance due on an account, through rebates of unearned finance charges or insurance premiums, or through amounts otherwise owed to or held for the benefit of the consumer ), the creditor shall : ( 1 ) Credit the amount of the credit balance to the consumer 's account ; ( 2 ) Refund any part of the remaining credit balance within seven business days from receipt of a written request from the consumer ; ( 3 ) Make a good faith effort to refund to the consumer by cash, check, or money order, or credit to a deposit account of the consumer, any part of the credit balance remaining in the account for more than six months. No further action is required if the consumer 's current location is not known to the creditor and can not be traced through the consumer 's last known address or telephone number.

( b ) Account termination.

( 1 ) A creditor shall not terminate an account prior to its expiration date solely because the consumer does not incur a finance charge.

( 2 ) Nothing in paragraph ( b ) ( 1 ) of this section prohibits a creditor from terminating an account that is inactive for three or more consecutive months. An account is inactive for purposes of this paragraph if no credit has been extended ( such as by purchase, cash advance or balance transfer ) and if the account has no outstanding balance. 

( c ) Timely settlement of estate debts ( 1 ) General rule.

( i ) Reasonable policies and procedures required. For credit card accounts under an open-end ( not home-secured ) consumer credit plan, card issuers must adopt reasonable written policies and procedures designed to ensure that an administrator of an estate of a deceased accountholder can determine the amount of and pay any balance on the account in a timely manner.

( ii ) Application to joint accounts. Paragraph ( c ) of this section does not apply to the account of a deceased consumer if a joint accountholder remains on the account.

( 2 ) Timely statement of balance ( i ) Requirement. Upon request by the administrator of an estate, a card issuer must provide the administrator with the amount of the balance on a deceased consumer 's account in a timely manner.

( ii ) Safe harbor. For purposes of paragraph ( c ) ( 2 ) ( i ) of this section, providing the amount of the balance on the account within 30 days of receiving the request is deemed to be timely.

( 3 ) Limitations after receipt of request from administrator ( i ) Limitation on fees and increases in annual percentage rates.
